name: Street Custom 'Choir Boy' Ultrasonic Emitter
description: A handheld ultrasonic weapon cobbled from salvaged industrial cleaning equipment and a focusing horn fashioned from sheet metal. The Choir Boy emits a concentrated beam of ultrasonic energy at frequencies between 20-40 kHz, causing intense pain, disorientation, and at close range, tissue damage to soft organs. The name comes from the high-pitched whine the device produces at the edge of human hearing — a sound operators describe as angelic right before it becomes agonizing. Build quality varies from surprisingly sophisticated to genuinely dangerous to the user.
specifications: frequency: 20-40 kHz variable power output: 140-160 dB depending on build effective range: 3-15 meters directional power source: Salvaged industrial battery packs weight: 1.2-2.5 kg operation time: 30-90 seconds continuous before overheating
story_hooks: A wave of Choir Boy attacks in Tier 1 has left dozens with permanent hearing damage — someone is distributing pre-built units for free along with target lists.

A modified Choir Boy has been tuned to interfere with a specific frequency used by Diaspora neural interfaces, causing temporary disconnection — for some users, that disconnection is psychologically devastating.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist assemblage of salvaged industrial components — part cattle prod, part vintage microphone, part DIY synthesizer. The device has an aggressive, jury-rigged aesthetic with a flared horn mouth dominating the front. Despite its cobbled appearance, there's an unsettling purposefulness to its design.
physical_description.dimensions: 38-42 cm in length, 12-16 cm horn diameter, 8-10 cm grip depth
physical_description.weight_description: Noticeably heavy in the hand — top-weighted from the horn assembly, requiring a firm two-handed grip. Feels unbalanced when held one-handed, with noticeable vibration during operation.
physical_description.primary_material: Salvaged stainless steel horn, reinforced polymer body, mixed-gauge electrical tubing, reclaimed industrial aluminum framework
physical_description.finish: Weathered brushed steel with oxidized patches, industrial-grade matte polymer body showing scuff marks and heat discoloration. Exposed wiring and battery junction points show corrosion and solder repair marks.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal grey horn with burnt-orange thermal scorching around the resonance chamber. Charcoal polymer grip with exposed copper and silver solder joints.
physical_description.grip_texture: Rough textured polymer with embedded grip tape, corroded metal friction points, occasional bare aluminum edges. Asymmetrical and ergonomically compromised depending on build variant.
distinctive_features: Large flared horn mouth with visible acoustic ridging and stress fractures
Exposed resonance chamber with heat-damaged insulation visible through cracks
Variable frequency tuning dial mounted on barrel — unmarked, requiring intuitive adjustment
Jury-rigged capacitor bank visible through semi-transparent polymer housing panel
Frayed power leads wrapped in degraded electrical tape at battery connection point
Vibration dampening coils wrapped around internal acoustic tube
Safety interlock button showing wear from repeated overrides
Thermal vents along barrel body with carbon scoring from sustained operation
Custom engraved text along grip: 'CHOIR BOY' in aggressive blocky lettering
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: No official branding. Faint industrial stencils from source equipment visible: partial 'INDUSTRIAL CLEANING' stamp on horn base. Handwritten serial number scratched into battery housing: illegible but present.
physical_description.condition_typical: Battle-worn and inconsistently maintained. Varying levels of cleanliness suggest multiple users or haphazard field repair. Some examples show fresh solder work alongside decades-old corrosion. Heat damage accelerates aging — most units show some thermal scarring after 50+ hours operation.
